 1   Q   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 2   A   I am testifying on behalf of the Regents of the New Mexico State University

 3       (“NMSU”).



 4   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY IN THIS

 5       PROCEEDING?

 6   A   The purpose of my Direct Testimony is to address the revenue deficiency that El

 7       Paso Electric Company (“EPE” or “Company”) claims in its Amended

 8       Application.    Specifically, I support several adjustments to EPE’s claimed

 9       deficiency.    As shown in the table below, based on revenue requirement

10       adjustments supported by me and other NMSU witnesses, EPE’s claimed revenue

11       deficiency of $70.483 million is overstated by at least $12.592 million. Stated

12       another way, with NMSU’s adjustments, EPE’s revenue requirement should

13       actually be reduced by at least $12.484 million.

 1   Q   ARE YOU SUPPORTING ANY EXHIBITS THAT ACCOMPANY YOUR

 2       DIRECT TESTIMONY?

 3   A   Yes. Exhibit JAL-1 is copy of the discovery responses I reference in my Direct

 4       Testimony. Exhibits JAL-2 and JAL-3 are my cash working capital and regulatory

 5       amortization adjustments, respectively.



 6                             II. CASH WORKING CAPITAL

 7   Q   DID YOU REVIEW EPE’S CASH WORKING CAPITAL (“CWC”)

 8       REQUIREMENTS?

 9   A   Yes. EPE proposes a CWC balance of negative $509,714 as shown on Schedule

10       A-03. This means EPE’s proposed CWC reduces the Company’s New Mexico

11       jurisdiction rate base.



12   Q   WHAT METHODOLOGY DID EPE USE TO QUANTIFY ITS CWC

13       BALANCE?

14   A   EPE uses a lead/lag study. Company witness Mr. Joseph S. Weiss supports the

15       lead/lag study that was used to develop the CWC factors that calculate the

16       Company’s CWC requirements.1 A lead/lag study measures the inflows and

17       outflows of cash that a company incurs to provide service to its customers. A

18       positive lead/lag study result represents funds that must be provided by a


         1
             Direct Testimony of Joseph S. Weiss (“Weiss Direct”) at 3.
                                                           Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                                                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT
                                                                                       Page 5



 1       company’s shareholders while a negative lead/lag study result represents funds that

 2       are provided by a company’s customers.

 3               The New Mexico jurisdiction negative $509,714 CWC balance is based

 4       on Mr. Weiss’s company-wide lead/lag study. The results of Mr. Weiss’s study

 5       were included as Exhibit JSW-2. The exhibit shows the company-wide CWC

 6       requirement is $267,983. The results of the company-wide study were allocated

 7       to New Mexico retail on EPE’s K Schedules.



 8   Q   WHAT IS CWC?

 9   A   CWC is the amount of cash necessary to finance the day-to-day operations of a

10       utility. CWC may be positive when it is shown that the utility’s shareholders

11       provide the financing for paying bills before billed revenues are collected from

12       customers. CWC may be negative when customers pay the utility more promptly

13       than when the utility is required to pay its bills. Broadly speaking, a CWC

14       requirement is calculated as a comparison between a revenue lag and an expense

15       lag. Revenue lag measures the number of days between when a utility provides

16       service to a customer and the date payment was received from that customer.

17       Similarly, expense lag is the time it takes a utility to pay for a service.
                                                          Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                                                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT
                                                                                      Page 6



 1   Q   DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS WITH THE AMOUNT OF CWC

 2       REQUESTED BY EPE?

 3   A   Yes, I believe EPE significantly overstated its requested CWC balance, despite

 4       having a negative balance, because of two errors in the CWC study. First, EPE

 5       includes uncollectibles in the collection lag portion of its revenue lag calculation.

 6       Second, EPE includes a payment processing lag in its revenue lag but not a

 7       corresponding bank float in its expense lag.

 8                  With these errors corrected, EPE’s company-wide CWC balance is

 9       reduced from $267,983 to about negative $17,944,327. This result is summarized

10       on my Exhibit JAL-2. This reduction in EPE’s CWC (and the corresponding

11       decrease in EPE’s rate base) decreases EPE’s New Mexico jurisdiction revenue

12       requirement by approximately $1.595 million at my colleague Mr. Gorman’s

13       proposed rate of return, grossed up for income taxes.



14   Q   WHAT REVENUE LAG DOES EPE PROPOSE?

15   A   Mr. Weiss explains that EPE’s revenue lag has four components: (1) service lag;

16       (2) billing lag; (3) collection lag; and (4) payment processing lag.2 Mr. Weiss

17       defines each component on pages 8 to 10 of his direct testimony. As explained

18       above, my issues are with the collection lag and payment processing lag

19       components. Table 2 shows Mr. Weiss’s calculation of EPE’s revenue lag.

6          calculation to account for the fact that those account receivable balances include

6   EPE’s proposal to not adjust its revenue lag for uncollectibles increases the

 8       The adjustment described above, to reflect a three-year average, increased EPE’s

 9       uncollectible expense (or bad debt expense). EPE is asking customers to pay both

14                  Removing the effects of uncollectibles reduces EPE’s revenue lag by

 1   A   My adjustment to correct EPE’s revenue lag is shown on Exhibit JAL-2. I

 2       recommend a weighted retail and wholesale revenue lag of about 39.5 days, or

 3       about 8.4 days less than Mr. Weiss’s 47.9 days. My exhibit updates EPE’s Exhibit

 4       JSW-2 with the corrected revenue lag. My adjustments combined lower EPE’s

 5       Company-wide CWC balance from $267,983 to about negative $17,944,327, or a

 6       reduction of about $18,212,310. Since my adjustment was applied to each cost

 7       category on Exhibit JSW-2, I recommend lowering EPE’s New Mexico

 8       jurisdictional CWC balance by $18,212,310. This adjustment lowers EPE’s New

 9       Mexico jurisdiction revenue requirement by approximately $1.595 million at my

10       colleague Mr. Gorman’s proposed rate of return, grossed up for income taxes.



11                         III. REGULATORY AMORTIZATIONS

12   Q   DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS WITH THE RECOVERY PERIOD EPE

13       PROPOSES FOR CERTAIN COSTS?

14   A   Yes.      EPE proposes a two-year recovery period for certain costs under its

15       Adjustment Nos. 10 (Regulatory Commission Expenses) and 13 (Amortization of

16       Regulatory Assets). For example, EPE is requesting to recover the costs of this

17       rate case over two years.8 Similarly, EPE is requesting recovery of its deferred

18       COVID-19 expenses over two years.9 These adjustments are primarily supported




         8
             Direct Testimony of Julissa Reza (“Reza Direct”) at 9.
         9
             Direct Testimony of Steven Sierra (“Sierra Direct”) at 57.
                                                         Direct Testimony of James A. Leyko
                                                          NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT
                                                                                   Page 14



 1       by EPE witnesses Julissa I. Reza and Steven A. Sierra. The Company also

 2       provided information on these costs in response to Discovery Request NMSU 4-

 3       27.10

 4               I recommend the Commission reject EPE’s proposed two-year recovery

 5       and instead direct the Company to recover these costs over three years.

 6   Q   PLEASE EXPLAIN.

 7   A   EPE’s last base rates were approved by the Commission in Case No. 20-00104-

 8       UT and initially went into effect on July 1, 2021.11 The current rates went into

 9       effect on January 1, 2024 after the Remand Order in Case No. 20-00104-UT.12

10       This means EPE’s rates will have been in effect for at least three years by the time

11       new rates are approved.

12               EPE’s rate case and other expenses in Adjustment Nos. 10 and 13 should

13       be recovered over the period rates approved in this proceeding will likely be in

14       effect. Therefore, it is important to look at the cadence in which EPE typically

15       files rate cases. If the Commission approves a two-year amortization and EPE’s

16       rates are in effect for longer than two years (as EPE’s current rates have been),

17       then this will allow EPE to over-recover these costs.

18               I recommend the Commission direct EPE to amortize its rate case

19       expenses over three years. This protects both EPE and its ratepayers. If EPE files

 2       not fully recovered, then the Company has the opportunity to request to include

 3       the unamortized balance of the expenses in cost of service in its next rate case.



 4   Q   YOU RECOMMEND A THREE-YEAR RECOVERY OF RATE CASE

 5       EXPENSES, WHAT DO YOU RECOMMEND FOR EPE’S DEFERRED

 6       COVID-19 EXPENSES?

 7   A   I recommend three years for these costs as well. EPE’s Exhibit CSP-3 shows the

 8       deferred COVID-19 expenses were incurred over a little more than three years.

 9       Thus three years is closer to the time period over which the costs accumulated

10       (compare to EPE’s recommendation of two years) and it aligns with the likely

11       period between EPE’s rate cases. Therefore, instead of recovering these costs over

12       two years, the Company should recover these costs over three years. Importantly,

13       I am not recommending the Company not recover these costs. Rather, I am

14       recommending the Commission extend the recovery period to align with the time

15       since EPE last filed a base rate case.



16   Q   DOES YOUR RECOMMENDED THREE-YEAR RECOVERY PERIOD

17       APPLY TO OTHER REGULATORY ASSETS?

18   A   Yes. I also recommend a three-year recovery of three other regulatory assets

19       included in EPE’s Adjustment No. 13: EPE’s deferred Western Energy Imbalance

 2       Remand costs; and deferred New Mexico Automated Metering System Time

 5   A   My adjustment is included as Exhibit JAL-3. Moving from a two-year recovery

 6       to a three-year recovery for the items identified above lowers EPE’s claimed

 7       revenue deficiency by approximately $1.248 million.



 8                               IV. CONCLUSION

 9   Q   DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

10   A   Yes, it does.

 8   Q   PLEASE       SUMMARIZE           YOUR       EDUCATIONAL           BACKGROUND            AND

10   A   I received a Bachelor of Arts Degree in History from Tulane University in 2007. I attended

11       Saint Louis University and received a Master of Business Administration Degree in 2011. I

18       several regulated utility matters as a Consultant for BAI. These assignments included revenue

20       the impact of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, and resource planning.

21               BAI was formed in April 1995. BAI and its predecessor firm have participated in more

22       than 700 regulatory proceedings in 40 states and Canada.
